items.q: Where is most of Earth’s phosphorus stored?
options: In rock and sediment
In the atmosphere as a gas
In living plants and animals
In rivers, lakes and the ocean

why.correct: Phosphorus is stored mainly in phosphate minerals in rock and in ocean sediments; it has no significant gas form.
options: Right: rock and sediment are the main reservoirs.
Phosphorus has no significant gas phase, unlike carbon and nitrogen.
Living things hold a small, active share.
Water holds only small amounts at any time.

items.q: Why does phosphorus usually move through ecosystems more slowly than carbon or nitrogen?
options: It has no gas phase to carry it.
Plants do not need phosphorus to grow and reproduce.
It is released mainly by volcanoes, which erupt rarely.
Decomposers do not release it from dead plants and animals.

why.correct: Carbon and nitrogen move quickly through the atmosphere. Phosphorus must be weathered from rock and moved by water, which is slow.
options: Right: no trip through the air makes it slow.
Plants need phosphorus for DNA, ATP and cell membranes.
Weathering of rock, not volcanoes, is the main source.
Decomposers do return phosphate to the soil.

items.q: Which process releases phosphate from rocks into the soil?
options: Weathering
Nitrogen fixation by bacteria
Photosynthesis
Denitrification in wet soil

why.correct: Rain, temperature changes and living things slowly break rock down, releasing phosphate.
options: Right: weathering frees phosphate from rock.
Fixation is part of the nitrogen cycle.
Photosynthesis moves carbon, not phosphate from rock.
Denitrification returns nitrogen gas to the air.

items.q: What do organisms use phosphorus for?
options: Building DNA, ATP, membranes and bones
Making the sugars of photosynthesis in leaves
Storing oxygen in the red cells of the blood
Breaking the strong bond in N2 gas from the air

why.correct: Phosphate is part of DNA and RNA, ATP (the energy carrier), the phospholipids of cell membranes, and the minerals of bones and teeth.
options: Right: DNA, ATP, membranes, bones and teeth.
Sugars are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Iron in blood carries oxygen, not phosphorus.
Bacteria break N2 with enzymes; that is not what phosphorus is for.

items.q: Phosphorus that settles in ocean sediments can return to land. How?
options: Sediments become rock that is slowly lifted up.
It rises from the sea as a gas and falls in rain.
Fish carry it up rivers and onto land each season.
Lightning fixes it from the air into the soil.

why.correct: Sediments harden into rock, and geologic uplift raises it, slowly, where weathering can release phosphate again.
options: Right: uplift of rock over geologic time.
Phosphorus has no significant gas phase, so it does not rise from the sea.
Animals move small amounts, such as seabird droppings, but not the main return route.
Lightning fixes nitrogen, not phosphorus.

items.q: Where does most of the phosphate in commercial fertilizer come from?
options: Mined phosphate rock
Phosphorus gas captured from the air
Bacteria living in the roots of legumes
Seawater that is boiled down to dry salt

why.correct: Phosphate fertilizer is made from mined phosphate rock, which forms far more slowly than it is mined.
options: Right: mined phosphate rock.
There is no phosphorus gas to capture.
Legume bacteria fix nitrogen, not phosphorus.
Seawater holds very little phosphate.

items.q: Phosphate sticks tightly to soil particles. How does most of the phosphate from a farm field reach a lake?
options: On soil washed off in heavy rain
As a gas blown over the lake by the wind
By denitrification in the wet soil of the field
Through the leaves of the crop and into the air

why.correct: Because phosphate clings to soil, it moves mostly when soil itself is washed away, so keeping soil on the field keeps phosphate out of water.
options: Right: phosphate rides on soil that washes away.
Phosphorus has no gas form.
Denitrification is part of the nitrogen cycle.
Leaves do not deliver phosphate to lakes.

items.q: A lake receives wastewater with high phosphate. Build the chain for what happens to the algae.

why.correct: Phosphate is usually the limiting nutrient in freshwater, so adding it lets algae grow fast.

specific.frame: Phosphate is often the ___ in lakes, so adding it makes algae ___, because ___.

role.label: Role of phosphate
options: limiting nutrient
main gas in the air
cause of denitrification

why.1: Phosphorus has no significant gas form.

direction.label: Algae
options: grow quickly
die off at once
stay the same

why.1: Adding a scarce nutrient helps algae grow, at least at first.
why.2: A limiting nutrient changes growth when it is added.

because.label: Reason
options: the scarcest nutrient is no longer in short supply
phosphate blocks sunlight
phosphate is a poison to fish

why.1: Phosphate is dissolved and does not block light.
why.2: The question is about algae growth, and phosphate is a nutrient for them.

specific.model: Phosphate is often the limiting nutrient in lakes, so adding it makes algae grow quickly, because the nutrient that was in shortest supply is no longer scarce.

items.q: Which ponds grew the most algae?
options: Ponds D, with both added
Ponds A, with no nutrient added
Ponds B, with nitrate added each week
Ponds C, with phosphate added each week

why.correct: Ponds D reached 31 µg/L, the highest value.
options: Right: 31 µg/L.
Ponds A had the least (4 µg/L).
Ponds B had 5 µg/L, barely more than A.
Ponds C had 28 µg/L, close to D but lower.

items.q: Which nutrient was limiting algae growth in these ponds?
options: Phosphate: it raised algae 4 to 28
Nitrate, since adding it raised algae from 4 to 5
Neither one, since algae need just light and water
Both equally, since ponds D have the most algae

why.correct: Phosphate alone gave a large rise; nitrate alone gave almost none. So phosphate was in shortest supply.
options: Right: adding phosphate made the big difference.
A rise of 1 µg/L is tiny compared with phosphate’s 24.
Nutrients clearly changed growth.
D is only a little above C, so phosphate did most of the work.

items.q: How many times more algae grew in ponds C than in ponds A?

mistakes.why: 24 µg/L is the difference. "How many times more" asks for the ratio: 28 / 4.
You divided A by C. Put the ponds you compare (C) on top: 28 / 4.

items.q: What is the purpose of ponds A in this study?
options: A baseline for comparison
They test the effect of adding both nutrients at once.
They show how fast phosphate is weathered from rock.
They are spare ponds in case another pond fails.

why.correct: Ponds A had nothing added, so they show how much algae grows without the treatment: the control.
options: Right: the control is a baseline for comparison.
Ponds D test both nutrients.
Weathering is not measured.
A control is part of the design, not a spare.

items.q: About how much phosphate does the farmland stream carry?
options: About 0.18 mg/L
About 0.02 mg/L
About 0.11 mg/L
About 1.8 mg/L

why.correct: The farmland bar reaches about 0.18 mg/L.
options: Right: just under 0.2 mg/L.
0.02 mg/L is the forest stream.
0.11 mg/L is the town stream.
The axis tops out at 0.2 mg/L.

items.q: What best explains why the forest stream has the least phosphate?
options: Roots hold the soil in place.
Forest leaves remove phosphate gas from the air.
Trees release their phosphate into the air as a gas.
Forest soil lacks phosphate, so little can wash in.

why.correct: Phosphate travels mostly on soil that washes away; forest cover keeps soil in place, and no fertilizer is added.
options: Right: little erosion and no fertilizer.
There is no phosphate in the air to remove.
Phosphorus has no gas form.
Forest soils contain phosphate; it just stays put.

items.q: How much more phosphate does the farmland stream carry than the forest stream, in mg/L?

mistakes.why: 9 is the ratio (0.18 / 0.02). "How much more, in mg/L" asks for the difference.

items.q: Which action would most directly lower phosphate in the farmland stream?
options: Winter cover crops on the fields
Adding more phosphate fertilizer just before heavy rain
Removing the trees that grow along the stream banks
Plowing the fields right before the winter storms

why.correct: Plant cover holds soil, and phosphate moves on soil. Less soil lost means less phosphate in the stream.
options: Right: keeping soil in place keeps phosphate out of the water.
More fertilizer before rain adds phosphate.
Trees along the bank catch soil; removing them adds phosphate.
Bare plowed soil washes away in storms.
